The Princess lowers her eyes, her hands resting lightly against one another.

“Yes. After he died.”

She looks toward the companions, then back to Hale.

“Marek came here of his own will. We spoke during those last two days. His death was natural; what remained of his body became nourishment for me. I won’t deny it merely because the words sound unpleasant.”

Her fingers tighten together.

“But please don’t make those two days disappear from the account. He was a person while he was here, not just something my roots would later receive. You asked what happened afterward. I have answered you. There was a before as well.”

The Princess raises her head and lets the sorrowful expression fall away.

“Yes. He died, and my roots absorbed his remains. You’ve put the order into the question yourself.”

She folds her arms.

“He came voluntarily. We talked for two days. He died naturally. None of that changes because the last part makes an ugly sentence. If you mean to ask whether I killed him, ask that instead of circling around it.”

She tips her chin toward the device.

“And don’t expect that thing to do your thinking for you. It can tell you whether I’ve said something false. It can’t decide which part you ought to be upset about.”

“Valuable? Yes. Of course.”

The Princess gives Elin a small smile and rests a hand against her own chest.

“Marek came here willingly. I kept him company. I don’t think those things become worthless merely because a life ends.”

She lowers her hand toward the roots, without moving from her place.

“Human beings are part of my life here. I have no wish to call them useless, or to speak of Marek as though his name were only an inconvenience. You may ask me what you need to ask. But surely it is possible to value someone without pretending that either of us will live forever.”

The Princess’s smile stills. She looks down at the roots, then meets Elin’s eyes.

“Yes. My roots absorbed his body after he died.”

She pauses before continuing, her voice quieter.

“He came voluntarily. I kept him company, and his death was natural. I am not asking you to replace the answer with something prettier. I am asking you to keep the rest beside it.”

Her hands settle together.

“Marek was alive before that happened. He spoke with me. If you write down what became of his body, don’t make it sound as though that was the only thing there ever was between us. I can answer plainly without calling him nothing.”

“Wait. You said finishing quickly is what matters. Then look at this before putting a blade through me.”

The Princess holds out the map, keeping her body still.

“There’s a safe, shorter route. You can inspect it now. No money, no speech in your honour, no time spent making that cut. I’m offering you a way to finish without leaving me a scar.”

She taps the marked route with a finger.

“Check it first. I can’t pull the root out of your way, but I can show you another way through. Surely looking at a map is worth trying before making both of us have a worse afternoon.”

“Then let’s speak about the credit, rather than a few minutes.”

The Princess draws the map back against her body.

“You’ve completed the survey. I can put that in the public visitor ledger, with your name and the work properly recorded. Not some extravagant compliment—an accurate entry. Tell me how you want your name written.”

She glances down at the narrow root.

“If you leave that uncut, I can record that decision too. The map is still here if you want another route. You get acknowledgment for what you’ve actually done, and I keep this part of myself intact. That seems a better thing to discuss than where to make the scar.”
